The attack failed, and I got the wording from the page source rather than from a rendering of it. A plain fetch of the Wikisource page was declined by the fetch model, so I pulled the raw wikitext of Page:Wittgenstein - Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, 1922.djvu/189 with curl (?action=raw) and read the proofread transcription of the 1922 Kegan Paul page directly. 6.4311 comes back as: 'Death is not an event of life. Death is not lived through.' then, as its own paragraph, 'If by eternity is understood not endless temporal duration but timelessness, then he lives eternally who lives in the present.' then 'Our life is endless in the way that our visual field is without limit.' The proposed quotation is the middle paragraph, verbatim, with nothing trimmed.

THE TRANSLATION IS THE DECISIVE TEST AND IT PASSES. This is the one line of the four where translation drift was a live danger, because the Tractatus has two standard English texts and they are not close here. Pears and McGuinness (1961) render the same remark 'If we take eternity to mean not infinite temporal duration but timelessness, then eternal life belongs to those who live in the present.' — different verb, different subject, different everything except the thought. The proposal's wording is not that; it is the Ogden wording, and the source line names Ogden. I did not rely on the quoted sentence alone to establish which text I was in: the two neighbouring sentences on the same page are distinctively Ogden too ('Death is not lived through' where Pears and McGuinness have 'we do not live to experience death'; 'Our life is endless in the way that our visual field is without limit' where they have 'our life has no end in just the way in which our visual field has no limits'). Three sentences in one Ogden shape, from the page image transcription of the 1922 edition. The translator credit is right.

LOCATOR CONFIRMED. 6.4311 it is, sitting between 6.431 ('As in death, too, the world does not change, but ceases.') and 6.4312 (the long remark on temporal immortality), both of which I read on the same page. The decimal numbering is the work's own, so it is the strongest form of locator available and needs no page number beside it.

WHAT I TRIED AND COULD NOT MAKE STICK. (1) The brief's Wittgenstein trap. The famous roving Wittgenstein line is 'The limits of my language mean the limits of my world', which the August Calendar For Life candidate list carries at cflId 236 (AUGUST-4, Salzburg Festival). This is not that line and is nowhere near it, so there is no collision of wording. I flag the adjacency for the editor only as a same-month, same-person risk: if the month also lands the Calendar For Life Wittgenstein, rule 8's no-person-twice-in-a-month bars one of them. That is an editing decision about the month, not a defect in this citation. (2) Speaker: none to name; the Tractatus has no characters. (3) Misattribution: not on the trap list; this is a numbered remark in a named work. (4) Scope: 1921 German, 1922 English, long before 1999; not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory.

PUBLISHABILITY AND SIX A.M. Rule 11 and rule 3 are the real questions here, because the remark this sentence belongs to opens with two flat sentences about death, and a reader who knows the Tractatus will hear them behind it. The proposal does not quote them, and taken alone the sentence contains no death, no wound and nothing needing a warning: it is a definition of eternity that hands the reader the present moment. For a month on impermanence that is close to the ideal philosopher's line — it is the one that says what stays, and says it without consolation-language. It clears both rules.

A NOTE THE EDITOR MAY WANT. The note field is empty. Unlike the other three I would leave it empty here: any gloss would have to mention the death sentences to be honest about the context, and that would import into the card exactly what quoting the middle paragraph alone keeps out.
